content.title: Managing Addons with Operators (Or How We Dropped Untested bash/sed for Go)
content.author: Jeff Johnson & Justin Santa Barbara
content.summary: The session explains how to replace fragile bash‑based add‑on deployment scripts with robust Kubernetes Operators, covering dependency management, rolling upgrades, configuration, and health checking for core add‑ons like kube‑dns. This matters because it modernizes add‑on management, improves reliability, and enables better lifecycle control for Kubernetes clusters.
content.description: Kubernetes has long deployed core components like kube-dns by running kubectl apply every few minutes from a directory on a master node. This worked great with simple addons on a single master node. content.summary: The session details how the team built an automated CI/CD test harness to benchmark Kubernetes at massive scale, revealing real performance and scalability limits of the control plane, kubelet, and cluster density. This helps operators understand and validate the scaling capabilities of their own deployments.

content.title: Shopify’s $25k Bug Report, and the Cluster Takeover That Didn’t Happen
content.author: Greg Castle
content.summary: The session walks through a real-world security incident where a researcher exploited a microservice to read Google Cloud metadata, potentially compromising the whole cluster. It shows how Shopify responded, used Kubernetes audit logs to trace the breach, and shares hardening practices and audit log queries to detect similar attacks.
content.description: In May, a security researcher reported a vulnerability in a Shopify microservice and demonstrated how it could be used to access keys from the Google Cloud metadata API. This could have led to a cluster takeover, for which Shopify awarded $25k through its bug bounty program. Shane will share his experience responding to the report, analyzing Kubernetes audit logs, and hardening the cluster to block the escalation path.
